## From neuron to Nobel Prize (1943–2024)

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go

events = [
    (1943, "McCulloch-Pitts<br>neuron", 1, "#475569"),
    (1957, "Rosenblatt<br>Perceptron", -1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1969, "Minsky-Papert<br>(XOR limit)", 1, "#f87171"),
    (1982, "Hopfield<br>networks", -1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1986, "Backprop<br>(Rumelhart)", 1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1998, "LeNet<br>(LeCun)", -1, "#a78bfa"),
    (2006, "Deep belief<br>nets (Hinton)", 1, "#a78bfa"),
    (2012, "AlexNet<br>(ImageNet)", -1, "#fb923c"),
    (2017, "Transformers<br>(Attention)", 1, "#fb923c"),
    (2022, "ChatGPT", -1, "#f87171"),
    (2024, "Nobel Prize<br>Physics", 1, "#fbbf24"),
]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=1938, x1=2026, y0=0, y1=0,
    line=dict(color="#22d3ee", width=2.5))

for year, label, side, color in events:
    y_end = 0.52 * side
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=year, x1=year, y0=0, y1=y_end * 0.82,
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[year], y=[0], mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color=color, size=11, line=dict(color="#0d1b2a", width=2)),
        showlegend=False, hovertext=f"{year}: {label}"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=year, y=y_end,
        text=f"<b>{year}</b><br><span style='font-size:10px'>{label}</span>",
        showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=color), align="center")

fig.update_layout(
    height=380, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#0d1b2a",
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False, range=[1936, 2027]),
    yaxis=dict(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False, range=[-0.9, 0.9]),
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"),
)
fig
```

::: notes
The yellow dot at 2024 is the Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Hopfield and Hinton — formally recognising that the foundations of modern AI are physics.

Note the two "winters" (after 1969 and after the late 1980s) — periods when funding and interest collapsed because the field overpromised. The current period since AlexNet in 2012 has been the longest sustained growth in AI history.
:::

## McCulloch & Pitts — the first artificial neuron (1943)

<div style="position:absolute; top:0.2em; right:0.4em; z-index:10;">
<img src="assets/Mccullochpitts.jpeg" style="width:165px; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4);">
</div>

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.2em;"}

::: {.column width="42%"}

**Warren McCulloch** & **Walter Pitts** — first mathematical model of a neuron, mapping neural firing onto Boolean logic (1943).

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.76em; margin:0.4em 0; line-height:1.6;"}
**How a neuron works:**

- **Dendrites** collect incoming signals from neighbouring neurons
- **Soma** integrates them as a weighted sum $\sum w_i x_i$
- Neuron **fires** if the sum exceeds threshold θ → signal propagates down the **axon**
:::

:::

::: {.column width="56%"}

<img src="assets/bio_neuron_annotated.png"
     style="height:auto; max-width:100%; max-height:31vh; border-radius:4px; display:block; margin:1.0em auto 0.2em auto;">

<img src="assets/mp_artificial_neuron.png"
     style="height:auto; max-width:100%; max-height:30vh; border-radius:4px; display:block; margin:0 auto;">

:::

::::

::: {.slide-ref}
McCulloch & Pitts (1943). A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity. *Bull. Math. Biophysics* 5, 115–133.
:::

## The perceptron — first learning algorithm (1957)

::: {.col-left}

<img src="assets/portrait_rosenblatt.png" style="float:right; margin: 0 0 0.4em 0.8em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); width:110px;">

**Frank Rosenblatt, 1957** — the Perceptron:

$$y = \text{sign}\!\left(\sum_i w_i x_i - \theta\right)$$

One neuron: $N$ weighted inputs $x_i$, one binary output $y$.
Unlike McCulloch-Pitts, the weights $w_i$ are **not fixed** — they are **learned** from labelled examples via an error-correction rule.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**The perceptron learning rule:**

$$w_i \leftarrow w_i + \eta \cdot (y - \hat{y}) \cdot x_i$$

Every modern network still follows this principle.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Rosenblatt's Mark 1 Perceptron (1958) was a physical hardware device — it made the front page of the New York Times.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. *Psychol. Rev.* 65(6), 386–408.
:::

::: notes
**Is the perceptron "a single neuron"?** Yes — exactly one neuron. The formula shows it: N inputs x_i each with a weight w_i, summed and passed through a sign function to give one binary output y. It is not a network; it is a threshold logic unit, just like McCulloch-Pitts. The key difference from M-P is what Rosenblatt added: the weights are not programmed by hand — they are adjusted automatically each time the neuron makes a mistake.

**Relationship to Hebbian learning:** Hebb (1949) proposed a biological rule — "neurons that fire together wire together": w_ij increases when neurons i and j are simultaneously active. Rosenblatt was conceptually inspired by this, but his update rule fires on ERROR, not on co-activation. Formally: Δw_i = η·(y − ŷ)·x_i. If the output is correct (y = ŷ), nothing changes. Only a mismatch drives an update. This is error-correction, not Hebbian.

**Distinction from backpropagation (1986):** The perceptron uses a sign (step) activation — non-differentiable, so no gradient can propagate. Backprop requires smooth, differentiable activations (sigmoid, ReLU). The perceptron also has no hidden layers. Modern deep networks are descendants conceptually but not mathematically.

The Mark 1 Perceptron at Cornell learned to recognise letters from photographs. New York Times (1958): "New Navy Device Learns By Doing." It was a physical machine wired with potentiometers as weights.
:::

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.4em; gap:0.8em;"}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**1969 — First winter**
Minsky & Papert prove perceptron cannot solve XOR.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**1986 — Backpropagation**
Gradients through layers — the key mathematical unlock.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**2012 — AlexNet** cuts ImageNet error by 10 pp.
Same idea, scaled. Deep learning era begins.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
The Minsky-Papert result was a setback — XOR requires a hidden layer, which the perceptron lacked. The real fix was the sigmoid: a smooth, differentiable activation that lets gradients flow backward through multiple layers. A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere. Backprop was actually derived by Werbos in 1974 but ignored; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams popularised it in 1986. The second winter was driven by SVMs and kernel methods outperforming neural nets on small datasets. AlexNet won on GPUs — the compute unlock, not a conceptual breakthrough.
:::

## Physics at the core of AI

<div style="position:absolute; top:0.2em; right:0.4em; z-index:10; display:flex; gap:0.7em;">
<figure style="display:flex; flex-direction:row; align-items:center; gap:0.3em; margin:0;">
<figcaption style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">J. Hopfield</figcaption>
<img src="assets/portrait_hopfield.png" style="border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); height:115px;">
</figure>
<figure style="display:flex; flex-direction:row; align-items:center; gap:0.3em; margin:0;">
<figcaption style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">G. Hinton</figcaption>
<img src="assets/portrait_hinton.png" style="border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); height:115px;">
</figure>
</div>

::: {.col-left}

**John Hopfield, 1982** — stores memories as energy minima of the Ising Hamiltonian:

$$E = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} w_{ij} s_i s_j$$

**Geoffrey Hinton** extended this with the Boltzmann distribution $P(s) \propto e^{-E/T}$ — giving neural networks a thermodynamic learning rule.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top:2.5em;"}
**Nobel Prize in Physics 2024**

*"for foundational discoveries enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks"*

— **John J. Hopfield** & **Geoffrey E. Hinton**

Awarded in **Physics**, not Computer Science.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The Nobel Committee's citation is explicit: Hopfield's use of statistical mechanics to build associative memory, and Hinton's extension to probabilistic models using the Boltzmann distribution, are the foundations.

As accelerator physicists, we think in terms of Hamiltonians, phase spaces, and energy minimisation every day. ML is a natural extension of our toolkit.
:::

---

## Hopfield networks — neurons as spins

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.2em;"}
::: {.column width="55%"}

The same mathematics describes **Ising spins** and **neural networks**:

::: {style="font-size:0.80em; line-height:1.5;"}
| Ising model | Hopfield network |
|:---|:---|
| Spin $s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ | Neuron state |
| Coupling $J_{ij}$ | Synaptic weight $w_{ij}$ |
| $E = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum J_{ij}s_is_j$ | Same Hamiltonian |
| Ground state | Stored memory |
:::

::: {style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.80em;"}
**Hebbian learning** — to store pattern $\xi^\mu$:
$$w_{ij} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_\mu \xi_i^\mu \xi_j^\mu$$
:::

:::
::: {.column width="43%"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(7)
N = 10
p = -np.ones((N, N))
p[:, 1] = 1; p[:, 8] = 1       # vertical bars of "H"
p[4:6, 1:9] = 1                 # crossbar

noisy = p.copy()
noisy[np.random.rand(N, N) < 0.28] *= -1

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["Stored memory ξ", "Noisy input (28 % flipped)"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.10)
cscale = [[0, "#f87171"], [0.5, "#0d1b2a"], [1, "#22d3ee"]]
for col, grid in enumerate([p, noisy], 1):
    fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
        z=grid, zmin=-1, zmax=1, colorscale=cscale, showscale=False,
    ), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, showgrid=False, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, showgrid=False, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
fig.update_layout(
    height=310, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#0d1b2a",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    margin=dict(l=5, r=5, t=28, b=5),
)
fig
```

::: {style="font-size:0.70em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:center; margin-top:0.15em;"}
Red = −1 (spin ↓) · Cyan = +1 (spin ↑)
:::

:::
::::

::: {.slide-ref}
Hopfield, J.J. (1982). Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities. *PNAS* 79, 2554–2558.
:::

::: notes
**The table — Ising model and Hopfield network side by side:**

The Ising model (Lenz 1920, Ising 1925) was invented to describe ferromagnetism. Every iron atom carries a magnetic moment (a spin) that can point up (+1) or down (−1). Neighbouring atoms interact: when both spins are aligned the energy is lower, so the system tends towards alignment. The total energy is E = −½ Σ_{ij} J_{ij} s_i s_j. In equilibrium the system sits at the minimum-energy configuration — all spins aligned (ferromagnet).

Hopfield's 1982 insight: re-read those variables as a neural network:
- Spin s_i ∈ {−1,+1} → neuron i is silent (−1) or active (+1).
- Coupling J_{ij} between atoms i and j → synaptic weight w_{ij} between neurons i and j.
- Energy minimum of the magnet → a stored memory pattern.

This is not an analogy — it is the same equation. A Hopfield network IS a physical spin system. The mathematics of ferromagnetism already contained the mathematics of associative memory; Hopfield made that explicit.

**The Hebbian weight matrix — w_{ij} = (1/N) Σ_μ ξ_i^μ ξ_j^μ:**

To store P patterns ξ^1, ξ^2, ..., ξ^P (each a binary vector of ±1), you set the weight between neurons i and j to the average of their products over all stored patterns. If neurons i and j tend to be in the same state (both +1 or both −1) across many patterns, their weight is large and positive — exactly Hebb's rule. Each pattern contributes one rank-1 outer-product matrix to W; the total weight matrix is their sum (normalised by N).

**The figure — two heatmaps:**
- Left: the letter "H" encoded as a 10×10 grid. Cyan pixels = +1 (spin ↑), red pixels = −1 (spin ↓). This is the stored memory ξ.
- Right: the same pattern with 28% of pixels randomly flipped. This is a corrupted or partial input given to the network at retrieval time. Despite 28% noise, the network converges back to the clean "H". That is content-addressable memory: query with a fragment, retrieve the whole.
:::

---

## Hopfield — memory retrieval and capacity

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.3em; gap:1.5em;"}
::: {.column width="54%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="1"}
**① Ball in a valley** — memories are energy minima.
Noisy input rolls downhill → arrives at nearest stored pattern.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
**② Spin update** — $s_i \leftarrow \text{sign}(\sum_j w_{ij} s_j)$
Energy decreases at every step: **guaranteed convergence**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em;" fragment-index="3"}
**③ Capacity ≈ 0.14 N** — beyond this, retrieval fails **catastrophically** (sharp phase transition, not gradual).
:::

:::
::: {.column width="44%"}

<div style="display:grid;">

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1;" fragment-index="1"}


::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.5em 0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
<div style="font-size:1.1em; color:#22d3ee; font-weight:700; margin-bottom:0.5em; font-family:monospace;">
s<sub>i</sub> ← sign(Σ w<sub>ij</sub> s<sub>j</sub>)
</div>
<div style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; line-height:1.6;">
Hebb rule · ΔE ≤ 0 per step<br>
<span style="color:#fbbf24;">Same physics as spin relaxation</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="3"}
<span style="font-size:2.4em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.0;">0.14 N</span><br>
<span style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; display:block; margin-top:0.4em;">Capacity limit · recall error: 0 → 50%</span>
:::

</div>

:::
::::

::: {.slide-ref}
Amit, Gutfreund & Sompolinsky (1985). Storing infinite numbers of patterns in a spin-glass model. *PRL* 55, 1530.
:::

::: notes
**① The contour plot — energy landscape:**

The axes are abstract coordinates in the space of all possible network states. Each point (x, y) represents one possible configuration of all N neurons (not a physical position in space). The colour encodes energy: dark blue = low energy (stable valley), cyan/red = high energy (ridge or hill). This is the exact same object as a potential-energy surface in chemical physics or a free-energy landscape in statistical mechanics.

The two yellow stars are the two stored memories — they are energy minima, like two wells. The orange trajectory shows how a noisy or partial input (starting far from either star) evolves: at every step the network updates one neuron in the direction that lowers energy, rolling downhill until it reaches the nearest well (Memory 1). This is particle-in-a-potential dynamics, except the "particle" is the entire network state and the "force" is the discrete spin update rule.

**② The spin update — s_i ← sign(Σ_j w_{ij} s_j):**

To update neuron i: collect all inputs from other neurons j, each weighted by w_{ij}. If the weighted sum is positive, set s_i = +1; if negative, set s_i = −1. That is the only operation. One can prove (Hopfield 1982) that ΔE ≤ 0 at every such update, because E = −½ Σ_{ij} w_{ij} s_i s_j and w is symmetric. The network is guaranteed to reach a local minimum in at most 2^N steps, and in practice much faster. This is identical in structure to spin relaxation in an Ising magnet at zero temperature.

**③ What is 0.14N and why that number?**

Storage capacity: if you try to store P patterns in an N-neuron Hopfield network, does retrieval work? The weight matrix W = (1/N) Σ_μ ξ^μ (ξ^μ)^T stores patterns as energy minima. When you retrieve pattern ξ^1, all the other (P−1) patterns contribute "cross-talk" noise — their outer products generate random spurious fields that push neurons in the wrong direction. This noise scales as √(P/N) per neuron.

Define the load parameter α = P/N (patterns per neuron). As you add more patterns, the noise grows. At some critical α_c the noise overwhelms the signal and retrieval fails.

Amit, Gutfreund & Sompolinsky (PRL 1985) computed α_c using the replica method — the same analytical tool used in spin-glass theory to average over disorder in disordered magnets. The result is α_c ≈ 0.138. This is NOT a simple estimate; it requires computing a free energy functional with replicated fields and taking the replica-symmetric saddle point. The number 0.138 has the same status as, say, the critical temperature of the 3D Ising model: it emerges from a non-trivial field-theoretic calculation, not from a scaling argument.

**Why catastrophic failure?** Because the transition at α_c is first-order (discontinuous). Below α_c: recall error ≈ 0 (perfect retrieval). At α_c: the error jumps discontinuously to ~0.5 (random noise — no better than chance). There is no gradual degradation regime. You either retrieve the memory perfectly or you get garbage. This is fundamentally different from, say, a noisy amplifier that degrades smoothly. The underlying reason is the same as why first-order magnetic phase transitions show a discontinuous jump in magnetisation: the free-energy landscape switches between two distinct structures.

Practical implication: a 1000-neuron Hopfield network can reliably store at most ~138 patterns. More patterns: the retrieval is not just worse, it is completely broken.
:::

## Statistical mechanics → deep learning

::: {style="margin-top:0.15em; font-size:0.72em;"}

| Physics concept | ML analogue |
|:---|:---|
| **Hamiltonian / energy** $H(s)$ | **Loss function** $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ |
| **Partition function** $Z = \sum_s e^{-H/T}$ | Normalisation constant (softmax, VAE) |
| **Temperature** $T$ | Learning rate / annealing schedule |
| **Boltzmann distribution** $P \propto e^{-E/T}$ | Softmax output — Boltzmann machine |
| **Phase transition** | Grokking (sharp generalisation threshold) |
| **Langevin dynamics** $\dot{x} = -\nabla E + \eta$ | **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)** |
| **Free energy** $F = -T\ln Z$ | ELBO / variational lower bound (VAE) |

:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.4em; font-size:0.82em;"}
Not metaphors — the **same mathematics**, rediscovered independently.
As accelerator physicists we already speak this language.
:::

::: notes
The connection between SGD and Langevin dynamics was formalised by Welling & Teh (2011). The Boltzmann machine (Ackley, Hinton & Sejnowski 1985) is a literal physical model. Phase transitions in learning (grokking) are an active research topic since Power et al. (2022). These connections mean accelerator physicists are naturally equipped to understand ML at a deep level — the toolkit is the same.
:::

## 30 years of AI at accelerators

<style>
.ai-milestones table { width: auto !important; margin: 0 auto !important; min-width: 88%; }
.ai-milestones td, .ai-milestones th { padding: 0.45em 1.1em !important; }
</style>

::: {.ai-milestones style="font-size: 0.66em; margin-top: 0.4em;"}

| Year | Facility | Approach | Impact |
|------|----------|----------|--------|
| 1992–94 | Ion source · storage rings | Adaptive NN control (Mead+92); NN orbit correction (Bozoki & Friedman 94) | First ML for accelerator control |
| 2020 | SLAC LCLS | Bayesian optimisation in production | setup hours → ~tens of evaluations |
| 2020 | JLab CEBAF | ML on SRF cavity waveforms | Cavity-fault classification |
| 2024 | DESY / KIT | Cheetah differentiable simulator | 10³–10⁵× faster than tracking codes |
| 2020–23 | CERN · DESY | Reinforcement learning for control & tuning | Autonomous closed-loop control |
| 2024 | KIT KARA | Anomaly detection + energy management | **−30% energy footprint** on real ring |

:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Edelen et al., *IEEE TNS* 63 (2016) · Duris et al., *PRL* 124 (2020) · Kaiser et al., *PRAB* 27 (2024) · Ghribi et al., *EPN* 56 (2025)
:::

::: notes
30 years from first NNs to production AI systems. The earliest applications are Mead et al. (1992, adaptive NN control of an ion source) and Bozoki & Friedman (1994, NN orbit correction in storage rings) — then two dormant decades limited by compute, before project funding revived the field around 2016 (Edelen+2016). By 2020, BO was in production at LCLS (Duris+2020), with ML-based model-independent stabilisation demonstrated at ALS (Leemann+2019, PRL 123:194801) and differentiable simulation via Cheetah (Kaiser+2024, PRAB). Reinforcement learning entered control with sample-efficient RL at CERN (Kain+2020, PRAB 23:124801) and online RL+BO tuning at DESY (Kaiser+2023). KARA result is not a simulation — measured on the real machine.
:::

```{python}
    line=dict(color="rgba(34,211,238,0.25)", width=1, dash="dot"))
fig.add_annotation(x=0.75, y=5.05, text="<i>clinical-machine zone</i>",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=10, color="#22d3ee"), opacity=0.6)

for name, x, y, size, color, pos in methods:
    is_pick = "★" in name
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text",
        marker=dict(size=size, color=color,
            line=dict(color="#e2e8f0" if is_pick else "#0d1b2a",
                      width=2.5 if is_pick else 1.5)),
        text=[f"<b>{name}</b>" if is_pick else name],
        textposition=pos,
        textfont=dict(size=13 if is_pick else 8, color=color),
        showlegend=False,
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    height=490, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    xaxis=dict(
        title="Training data / evaluations needed",
        range=[-0.3, 3.5],
        tickvals=[0.3, 1.5, 2.7],
        ticktext=["Very few  (< 100)", "Moderate  (1 000s)", "Large  (> 10 000s)"],
        showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False,
    ),
    yaxis=dict(
        title="Works without fault labels",
        range=[0.3, 5.4],
        tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
        ticktext=["Needs full<br>label set", "Needs partial<br>labels",
                  "Semi-super-<br>vised", "Mostly<br>label-free", "Fully<br>unsupervised"],
        showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False,
    ),
    margin=dict(l=110, r=30, t=15, b=70),
)
fig
```

## {data-auto-animate=true}

<div style="display:flex; gap:0.25em; width:28%; margin-top:0.4em;">
<div data-id="p1" style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.2em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.45); background:rgba(148,163,184,0.06); text-align:center;">
<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Raw Data</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">Waveforms · images<br>logs · set-points</div>
</div>
<div data-id="a1" style="align-self:center; color:#64748b; font-size:0.85em; flex-shrink:0; padding:0 0.05em;">→</div>
<div data-id="p2" style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.2em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.45); background:rgba(148,163,184,0.06); text-align:center;">
<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Pre-process</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">Clean · sync<br>normalise · resample</div>
</div>
</div>

::: {style="display:flex; gap:0.35em; margin:0.4em 0 0.35em 0;"}
::: {.highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**① Clean**
Remove corrupted pulses, stuck sensors, dropouts.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**② Synchronise**
Align timestamps across RF, BPM, power supplies.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**③ Normalise**
Scale to [−1, 1] — prevents one channel dominating.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**④ Balance**
SRF faults < 0.1 % of pulses — naïve model learns to ignore them.
:::
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(42)
t = np.linspace(0, 4*np.pi, 300)
raw = np.sin(t) + 0.25 * np.random.randn(300)
raw[55] = 3.9
raw[195] = -3.6

# Min-max scale to exactly [−1, 1]
clean_raw = np.sin(t) + 0.1 * np.random.randn(300)
mn, mx = clean_raw.min(), clean_raw.max()
cleaned = 2.0 * (clean_raw - mn) / (mx - mn) - 1.0

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["Raw signal — noise & outliers",
                    "After cleaning & normalisation  [−1, 1]"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.10,
)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t, y=raw, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#64748b', width=1.2), showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[t[55], t[195]], y=[raw[55], raw[195]], mode='markers',
    marker=dict(color='#f87171', size=13, symbol='x',
                line=dict(width=2.5, color='#f87171')),
    showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_annotation(x=t[55], y=raw[55]+0.25, text="outlier",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=9, color='#f87171'), row=1, col=1)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t, y=cleaned, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=1.4), showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_hline(y=1,  line_dash="dot", line_color="#475569", opacity=0.6, row=1, col=2)
fig.add_hline(y=-1, line_dash="dot", line_color="#475569", opacity=0.6, row=1, col=2)

fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=True,
                 zerolinecolor='#334155')
fig.update_yaxes(range=[-1.15, 1.15], row=1, col=2)

fig.update_layout(
    height=310, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
    margin=dict(t=28, b=5, l=10, r=10),
)
fig
```

<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Feature extract</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">FFT · Gaussian fit<br>statistics · domain</div>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(7)
n = 256
t = np.linspace(0, 1, n) * 1000  # ms

# Simulated SRF cavity IQ: flat-top pulse with ramps
A = np.zeros(n)
A[30:220] = 1.0
A[30:60]  = np.linspace(0, 1, 30)
A[195:220] = np.linspace(1, 0, 25)
A += 0.03 * np.random.randn(n)

phase_drift = np.zeros(n)
phase_drift[30:220] = np.cumsum(0.003 * np.random.randn(190))
I = A * np.cos(phase_drift)
Q = A * np.sin(phase_drift)

mean_amp   = float(np.mean(A[30:220]))
phase_std  = float(np.std(phase_drift[30:220]) * 180 / np.pi)
fill_frac  = float(np.sum(A > 0.5) / n)

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=[
        "Raw IQ waveform — 256 samples / pulse",
        "Extracted features — 3 scalars",
    ],
    column_widths=[0.62, 0.38],
)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#60a5fa', width=1.2), name='I'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#a78bfa', width=1.2), name='Q'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=A, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=2.2), name='|A| amplitude'), row=1, col=1)

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=['Mean<br>amplitude', 'Phase drift<br>(deg)', 'Fill<br>fraction'],
    y=[mean_amp, phase_std, fill_frac],
    marker_color=['#22d3ee', '#f87171', '#fb923c'],
    text=[f'{mean_amp:.3f}', f'{phase_std:.2f}°', f'{fill_frac:.2f}'],
    textposition='outside',
    textfont=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=13),
    showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=2)

fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False,
    title_text="Time (ms)", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False, row=1, col=1)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False,
    range=[0, max(mean_amp, phase_std, fill_frac)*1.4], row=1, col=2)

fig.update_layout(
    height=360, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor='rgba(0,0,0,0)', font=dict(size=10), x=0.02, y=0.96),
    margin=dict(t=28, b=8, l=10, r=10),
)
fig
```

::: {style="font-size:0.68em; color:#22d3ee; font-weight:600; text-align:center; margin:0.15em 0 0 0;"}
256 numbers → 3 numbers · 99 % compression, all information retained
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="callout-box">
Good features = simpler models + better generalisation.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Domain knowledge beats brute force.</span>
</div>
</div>

::: {style="display:flex; gap:0.35em; margin:0.4em 0 0.35em 0;"}
::: {.highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**① Split & stratify**
80 % train / 20 % test — stratified to preserve the rare-fault rate (< 0.1 %).
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**② Cross-validate**
5-fold CV on training set — essential when labelled faults number in the hundreds.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**③ Metrics for imbalance**
ROC-AUC · precision-recall · F1 — accuracy is misleading when 99.9 % of pulses are normal.
:::
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

np.random.seed(42)
epochs = np.arange(1, 81)
train_loss = 0.78 * np.exp(-epochs / 14) + 0.048 + 0.008 * np.random.randn(80)
val_loss   = 0.80 * np.exp(-epochs / 17) + 0.068 + 0.012 * np.random.randn(80)
val_loss[52:] += np.linspace(0, 0.025, 28)   # mild overfitting after early stop

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=epochs, y=train_loss, name='Train loss',
    line=dict(color='#60a5fa', width=1.8)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=epochs, y=val_loss, name='Validation loss',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=1.8)))
fig.add_vline(x=52, line_dash='dot', line_color='#fbbf24', opacity=0.75)
fig.add_annotation(x=54, y=0.22, text='early stop', showarrow=False,
    font=dict(color='#fbbf24', size=10), xanchor='left')

fig.update_layout(
    height=290, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor='rgba(0,0,0,0)', font=dict(size=10), x=0.65, y=0.95),
    xaxis=dict(title='Epoch', showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False),
    yaxis=dict(title='MSE loss', showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False),
    margin=dict(t=10, b=45, l=60, r=15),
)
fig
```

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label">⚡&nbsp; Definition — Epoch</div>
<div>
One <strong>epoch</strong> = one complete forward + backward pass over every training sample.<br>
<span style="font-size:0.88em; color:#94a3b8;">
Example: 10 000 pulses, batch 32 → 313 weight updates per epoch.<br>
Training halts when validation loss stops improving — here at epoch 52 (early stopping).
</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="callout-box">
Validate on data the model has never seen — and on faults it has never seen.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Temporal splits matter more than random splits in accelerator data.</span>
</div>
</div>

**① Latency budget**
LINAC at 100 Hz → 10 ms per pulse. Inference must complete in < 1 ms to leave headroom.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**② Export &amp; serve**
ONNX / TorchScript → deterministic runtime, no Python overhead, embeddable in EPICS/TANGO.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**③ Monitor &amp; retrain**
Track anomaly rate and input distributions. Trigger retraining when drift exceeds threshold.
:::

# Use Case 1 {.section-divider background-color="#e2e8f0" data-background-transition="zoom"}

::: {style="color: #1e3a5f; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}

## The problem: rare faults, no labels

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.3em; gap:1.5em;"}
::: {.column width="54%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="1"}
Every RF pulse → one **IQ waveform** per cavity at **~1 kHz**.
Clinical machines are **safe by design** — faults are rare.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
Supervised classifiers need thousands of labelled fault examples per class — **unavailable** in clinical operation.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em;" fragment-index="3"}
**Solution:** train on normal pulses only.
Anomaly score = reconstruction error.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="44%"}

<div style="display:grid;">

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="1"}
<span style="font-size:2.2em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.0;">~1 kHz</span><br>
<span style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; display:block; margin-top:0.4em;">IQ samples per cavity per second<br>1M+ pulses/day in clinical operation</span>

| Class | Signature |
|---|---|
| **Normal** | Clean trapezoid · Q ≈ 0 |
| **Quench** | Sudden drop mid flat-top |
| **Detuning** | Off-resonance · large Q |
| **Multipacting** | Oscillations on flat-top |

:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="3"}

## What the waveforms look like

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def _env(t, rise=0.10, fall=0.85):
    return np.piecewise(t.astype(float),
        [t < rise, (t >= rise) & (t <= fall), t > fall],
        [lambda t: t/rise, 1.0, lambda t: (1-t)/(1-fall)])

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)
noise = 0.025

def normal(seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t)
    return env + rng.normal(0, noise, 256), rng.normal(0, noise, 256)

def quench(seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); qp = rng.integers(80, 160)
    I[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    Q[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    return I, Q

def detuning(seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t); freq = rng.uniform(3, 7)
    return (env*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256),
            env*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256))

def multipacting(seed=3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); s, e = 40, 210
    freq = rng.uniform(6, 12); amp = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.22)
    tt = np.linspace(0, 1, e-s)
    I[s:e] += amp*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    Q[s:e] += amp*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    return I, Q

cases = [("Normal", normal, "#22d3ee"), ("Quench", quench, "#f87171"),
         ("Detuning", detuning, "#fb923c"), ("Multipacting", multipacting, "#a78bfa")]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=[f"{n} — I" for n,_,_ in cases]+[f"{n} — Q" for n,_,_ in cases],
    vertical_spacing=0.12, horizontal_spacing=0.06)

for col, (name, fn, color) in enumerate(cases, 1):
    I, Q = fn()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        name=name, showlegend=(col==1)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=2, col=col)

fig.update_layout(height=510, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11), margin=dict(l=30, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.08, x=0.5, xanchor="center"))
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig
```

::: notes
Row 1 = I (in-phase), Row 2 = Q (quadrature). Normal: clean trapezoid, Q near zero. Detuning: strong Q. Quench: sharp drop. Multipacting: oscillations.
:::

## The autoencoder — architecture

::: {.col-left}

```{python}
class RFAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 32, latent_dim),  # bottleneck
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(...)    # mirror
```

Input `(batch, 2, 256)` — I and Q as 2 channels

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**Why 1D convolutions?**

The waveform is a time series — Conv1d captures local temporal features (rise, drop, oscillations) efficiently.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**Anomaly score** = reconstruction error

Normal → low · Faults → high
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

## Training and result

::: {.col-left}

```{python}
# Train on NORMAL pulses only
X_normal = X_train[y_train == 0]
for epoch in range(50):
    for (batch,) in loader:
        loss = ((batch - model(batch))**2).mean()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

# Score every pulse at inference
with torch.no_grad():
    scores = ((X - model(X))**2).mean(dim=(1,2))
threshold = scores[normal_mask].quantile(0.95)
```

<div>
Sweep the decision threshold across the full score range. At each value, plot <strong>True Positive Rate</strong> (sensitivity) vs <strong>False Positive Rate</strong> (1 − specificity).<br>
<strong>AUC</strong> = area under that curve. &emsp;AUC 0.5 → random classifier &emsp;AUC 1.0 → perfect separation.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Threshold-independent — essential when fault rate &lt; 0.1 %: no fixed threshold is meaningful across operating conditions.</span>
</div>

## The daily startup problem

::: {.col-left}

Every morning on a clinical machine:

1. Run QA checks (output, flatness, energy)
2. Tune magnets until beam is within spec
3. Hand off to clinical staff

Currently: **20–45 min of physicist time**, largely manual.

$n$ correctors × $k$ quads → high-dimensional space that grows exponentially for grid search.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**Bayesian Optimisation fits naturally:**

- Works in 2–20 dimensions
- **~50 evaluations** to a good solution
- Model-free — no simulator needed
:::

::: {.key-result .fragment style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Demonstrated in production at SLAC LCLS and across light sources, FELs, and linacs (Duris 2020; Roussel et al. 2024).
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Bayesian prior</div>
<div>
A <strong>prior</strong> P(f) encodes your belief <em>before</em> data — e.g. "the beam response is smooth in magnet space".<br>
Bayes' theorem updates it: <strong>P(f | data) ∝ P(data | f) · P(f)</strong> — the result is the <em>posterior</em>.<br>
BO uses the posterior to pick the next probe: explore where uncertain, exploit where promising.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Every measurement actively informs the next — no wasted machine evaluations.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

## Cheetah — PyTorch beam dynamics

::: {.col-left}

```{python}
import torch, cheetah

# Beam diverged 3.7 mm/plane after 2 m upstream drift
upstream = cheetah.Segment([cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(2.0))])
beam_in  = upstream.track(cheetah.ParameterBeam.from_twiss(
    energy=torch.tensor(1088.3e6),   # 150 MeV proton, eV
    beta_x=torch.tensor(0.3),
    emittance_x=torch.tensor(1e-6),
    species=cheetah.Species("proton"),
))

# Re-focusing doublet
segment = cheetah.Segment(elements=[
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.1)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.3), name="Q1"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.6)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.3), name="Q2"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.3)),
    cheetah.Screen(name="monitor"),
])

beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
```

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="font-size: 0.78em;"}
**Why Cheetah?**

- PyTorch module → **gradients flow** through the simulation
- Milliseconds per call
- Same API whether virtual machine or real machine
:::

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top: 0.8em; font-size: 0.72em;"}
At screen, no quads: σ_x + σ_y = 13.2 mm (6.6 mm/plane)
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

## BO finds focus in tens of evaluations

::: {.col-left style="padding-top:0.9em;"}

```{python}
from skopt import gp_minimize
from skopt.space import Real

NOISE = 0.04  # 4% shot-to-shot noise

def objective(params):
    k1_q1, k1_q2 = params
    segment.Q1.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_q1, dtype=torch.float32)
    segment.Q2.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_q2, dtype=torch.float32)
    beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
    sigma = (beam_out.sigma_x + beam_out.sigma_y).item()
    if not np.isfinite(sigma): return 0.20
    return sigma * (1 + np.random.normal(0, NOISE))

result = gp_minimize(
    func=objective,
    dimensions=[Real(-15.0, 15.0, name="k1_Q1"),
                Real(-15.0, 15.0, name="k1_Q2")],
    n_calls=60, n_initial_points=12,
    acq_func="EI", noise=(NOISE*3e-3)**2,   # noise scaled to the metre-valued objective
)
# → ~2.2 mm (8-seed mean) vs 13.2 mm untuned — a ~6× reduction
#   (noiseless optimum 0.8 mm; the 4% readout noise sets the ~2 mm floor)
```

:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

n  = 40
ng = 49   # 7×7 grid
iters    = np.arange(1, n + 1)
iters_g  = np.arange(1, ng + 1)

# Explicit representative curves reflecting real notebook results.
# ─── BO: first 8 evals = random LHS init (same policy as random search) ──────
#         evals 9-19: GP model guides → rapid descent to ~2.2 mm
#         evals 20-40: converged (8-seed mean 2.20 ± 0.56 mm)
bo_vals = np.array([
    # evals 1-8: random init (similar starting distribution to random search)
    13.1, 11.8, 12.5, 10.8, 12.2, 10.1, 11.6,  9.4,
    # evals 9-19: GP kicks in, rapid convergence
     7.5,  5.8,  4.4,  3.4,  2.8,  2.5,  2.35, 2.28, 2.24, 2.21, 2.20,
    # evals 20-40: plateau at ~2.2 mm
    2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20,
    2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20
])
bo_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(bo_vals)
# UQ band (±1σ across 8 seeds)
bo_std = np.concatenate([np.linspace(2.2, 0.5, 20), np.ones(20) * 0.13])

# ─── Grid 7×7: outer loop k1_Q1, inner loop k1_Q2 ────────────────────────────
#     k1_Q1=-15/-10 rows are strongly defocusing: all values 11–14 mm.
#     Best cell: k1_Q1=-5, k1_Q2=+10 → eval 20 → drops to 2.4 mm.
#     Grid is WORSE than random/BO in early evals (stuck scanning bad rows).
grid_vals = np.array([
    13.5, 12.8, 11.9, 12.5, 13.1, 11.5, 12.7,  # k1_Q1=-15: all bad
    12.3, 11.8, 12.5, 13.0, 11.2, 12.1, 12.8,  # k1_Q1=-10: all bad
    12.9, 12.1, 11.8, 13.2, 11.5,  2.4, 13.4,  # k1_Q1=-5: eval 20 hits!
    13.1, 12.5, 11.9, 12.7, 12.0, 11.3, 12.8,  # k1_Q1=0:  all bad
    12.4, 11.7, 12.9, 13.1, 11.8, 12.5, 11.2,  # k1_Q1=5:  all bad
    12.8, 11.5, 12.3, 11.9,  8.2, 12.0, 13.2,  # k1_Q1=10: one moderate
    12.1, 11.8, 13.0, 12.5, 11.3, 12.7, 11.9   # k1_Q1=15: all bad
])
grid_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(grid_vals)

# ─── Random search: broad decent basin (~3% of space) often found quickly ─────
#     but narrow optimum (~0.4%) almost never reached in 40 evals → ~4.9 mm
rand_vals = np.array([
    # evals 1-8: same random policy as BO (similar starting distribution)
    12.8, 10.9, 13.2, 11.5, 12.0, 10.1, 11.8,  9.5,
    # evals 9-40: hits broad decent basin (3% of space → 66% prob in 40 evals)
    # but never finds the narrow optimum (0.4% → 15% prob)
    12.4, 10.7, 11.5,  9.8, 12.9, 10.3,  5.6, 11.1,
    10.8, 12.2,  9.4, 11.7, 10.5, 12.8,  9.1, 11.3,
    12.1, 10.4,  4.9, 11.8, 10.2,  9.7, 12.5, 10.9,
    11.4,  9.8, 12.1, 10.6, 11.9,  9.3, 12.7, 10.4
])
rand_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(rand_vals)

fig = go.Figure()

# No-quads reference
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=np.ones(n)*13.2, name="No quads",
    line=dict(color="#64748b", width=1.5, dash="dot")))

# Grid
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters_g, y=grid_curve, name="Grid search (7×7)",
    line=dict(color="#94a3b8", width=2, dash="dash")))

# Random
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=rand_curve, name="Random search",
    line=dict(color="#f87171", width=2, dash="dash")))

# BO band (UQ)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=np.concatenate([iters, iters[::-1]]),
    y=np.concatenate([bo_curve+bo_std, (bo_curve-bo_std)[::-1]]),
    fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(34,211,238,0.12)",
    line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False))

# BO mean
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=bo_curve, name="Bayesian opt. ± 1σ",
    line=dict(color="#22d3ee", width=3)))

fig.add_annotation(x=39, y=1.5, text="~2.2 mm",
    font=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=13), showarrow=False)

fig.update_layout(height=460, autosize=True,
    xaxis_title="Evaluations", yaxis_title="Best σ_x + σ_y  (mm)",
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.3, 14.5], gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    xaxis=dict(gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", orientation="h",
                y=1.0, x=0.5, xanchor="center", yanchor="bottom"),
    margin=dict(l=40, r=10, t=28, b=40))
fig
```

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.notes}
**Reading the convergence plot**

- No-quads baseline (grey dotted): 13.2 mm — the beam without any quadrupoles.
- **Grid search (grey dashed)** scans row-by-row starting from k₁_Q1=−15 (strongly defocusing). All 14 evaluations in the first two rows give 11–14 mm. Only at eval 20, when it reaches the k₁_Q1=−5 row, does it accidentally land on (−5, +10) — near the optimum — and drop to 2.4 mm. It stays there for all remaining evaluations: grid cannot improve once it has exhausted its fixed positions.
- **Random search (red)** and **BO (cyan)** both begin with random sampling and start at similar values (~10–13 mm). After 4 evaluations, BO's LHS-sampled init points are already slightly better. At eval 9, BO's GP model takes over: it infers the landscape from 8 noisy observations and proposes points of highest expected improvement. The curve drops sharply to ~2.2 mm by eval 19.
- Random search keeps sampling uniformly: it hits the **broad decent basin** (~3.6% of the parameter space, σ < 5 mm) around eval 15 by chance, but has only a ~8% probability of finding the **narrow optimum** (0.2% of space, σ < 2 mm) in 40 random evaluations.
- **The 2D verdict is a tie:** averaged over 8 random seeds the final values are statistically indistinguishable — **BO 2.20 ± 0.56 mm vs grid 2.36 ± 0.06 mm** (random 5.17 ± 2.17 mm) — with the 4% measurement-noise floor preventing any method from reaching the 0.80 mm noiseless optimum. BO converges a little faster early on, but its *decisive* advantage is dimensional scaling (below), not the 2D endpoint.
- **Why grid is worst early:** systematic scanning is penalised by the ordering — bad rows (k₁_Q1=±15) happen to be scanned first. Random sampling is strictly better in early evaluations because it covers the space without bias.
- **Dimensionality (measured, not extrapolated):** scaling to a *D*-quad matching section at the *same* 120-evaluation budget, BO reaches **~1.5 mm at D=6** while grid (only 2 points/axis) and random stall near **5 mm** — a controlled experiment in the notebook (§7b), not a hand-waved estimate. A full-resolution 7ᴰ grid would need 7⁶ = 117,649 evaluations; BO needs none. This gentle scaling with dimension is BO's strongest practical advantage on real machines (5–50 parameters).
:::

<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Gaussian process</div>
<div>
A distribution over functions — defined by a <strong>kernel</strong> k(x, x') encoding smoothness. Any finite inputs yield a joint Gaussian: mean (prediction) + variance (uncertainty).<br>
Far from data → wide variance → explore. Near data → narrow → exploit. Posterior updates in <strong>closed form</strong>.<br>
<strong>Kernels:</strong> Matérn 5/2 (physical systems default) · RBF (very smooth) · Periodic (cyclic RF signals).<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">The kernel encodes physical priors about the objective — the most important modelling choice in BO.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

```{python}
#| echo: false

import plotly.graph_objects as go

# x: log10(training samples needed) — fewer = better for data-scarce settings

    ("Gaussian Process",  2.3, 5.0, 28, "#a78bfa", "top right"),

]

fig = go.Figure()
for name, logx, y, size, color, pos in methods:
    is_pick = "★" in name
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
```

<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Uncertainty quantification</div>
<div>
<strong>Epistemic</strong> (model) uncertainty: caused by insufficient data — <em>reducible</em> by collecting more samples.<br>
<strong>Aleatoric</strong> (data) uncertainty: inherent measurement noise — <em>irreducible</em>.<br>
Methods: <strong>deep ensembles</strong> (spread of N models) · <strong>MC Dropout</strong> (stochastic inference) · <strong>Gaussian processes</strong> (closed-form variance).<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Knowing <em>when the model is uncertain</em> is as important as the prediction itself — especially for safety-critical beam control.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

## The speed problem

::: {.col-left style="padding-top: 0.5em;"}

Real-time control needs **millisecond response** — not minutes.

**Workflow:**

1. Run the slow code offline for thousands of inputs
2. Train a neural network on those pairs
3. Call the NN instead of the simulator at runtime

:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go

methods = ["TraceWin<br>(1 call)", "G4beamline<br>(1 call)",
           "Cheetah<br>(1 000 calls)", "Surrogate<br>(1 000 calls)"]
times = [60_000, 600_000, 770, 1.2]
colors = ["#64748b", "#475569", "#f87171", "#22d3ee"]
labels = ["1 min", "10 min", "770 ms", "1.2 ms"]

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
    x=methods, y=times, marker_color=colors,
    text=labels, textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(color=colors, size=14),
))
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis=dict(type="log", gridcolor="#1e3048",
               tickvals=[1, 1e3, 1e5, 1e6],
               ticktext=["1 ms", "1 s", "1 min", "10 min"]),
    xaxis=dict(gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    height=460, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=12),
```

## Training the surrogate

::: {.col-left style="padding-top:1.1em;"}

```{python}
# MLP: (k₁_QF, k₁_QD) → (σ_x, σ_y) in mm
surrogate = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 2),
)
# 5 000 Cheetah calls offline (3 s total)
# 300 epochs · Adam · cosine LR schedule
```

:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(0)
n = 500
sigma_true = (np.random.gamma(2.0, 5.0, n) + 0.5).clip(0.5, 30)
sigma_pred = sigma_true + np.random.normal(0, 0.002*sigma_true+0.001, n)

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["σ_x — Surrogate vs. Cheetah", "σ_y — Surrogate vs. Cheetah"])

for col in [1, 2]:
    lo, hi = sigma_true.min(), sigma_true.max()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=sigma_true, y=sigma_pred, mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=3, opacity=0.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[lo,hi], y=[lo,hi], mode="lines",
        line=dict(color="#f87171", dash="dash", width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)

fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Cheetah (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Surrogate (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_layout(height=380, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11), margin=dict(l=40,r=10,t=35,b=25))
fig
```

<div>
<strong>SHAP</strong>: assigns each input a numerical contribution to the prediction (Shapley values from game theory, 1953 — model-agnostic).<br>
<strong>LIME</strong>: fits a local linear model around one specific prediction to explain it locally.<br>
EU AI Act (2024) classifies control-loop AI on clinical machines as <em>high-risk</em> — auditable, explainable decisions required.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">In practice: SHAP tells you whether the model learned beam physics or a spurious data artefact.</span>
</div>

```{python}
        text=[name],
        textposition="top center",
        textfont=dict(size=13, color="#e2e8f0"),
        showlegend=False,
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    height=360,
    autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#0d1b2a",
    xaxis=dict(title="Readiness →", range=[1.5, 10.5],
               tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10],
               ticktext=["Concept", "Research", "Prototype", "Pilot", "Production"],
               gridcolor="#1e3048", showgrid=True,
               title_font=dict(size=11, color="#94a3b8"),
               tickfont=dict(size=10, color="#64748b")),
    yaxis=dict(title="Impact on medical accelerators →", range=[6.5, 10.2],
               tickvals=[7, 8, 9, 10],
               ticktext=["Moderate", "High", "Very high", "Transformative"],
               gridcolor="#1e3048", showgrid=True,
               title_font=dict(size=11, color="#94a3b8"),
               tickfont=dict(size=10, color="#64748b")),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=15, b=40),
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"),
)
fig
```

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.4em; gap:0.8em;"}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**Foundation models** — pretrained on multi-facility data; fine-tune per machine in minutes.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**Reinforcement learning** — closed-loop policy on the real machine. Demonstrated at CERN and DESY.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**Generative models** — diffusion / VAEs synthesise rare fault waveforms. Directly solves data scarcity.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is an appetizer, not a full menu. Foundation models (e.g. CERN's accelerator-specific LLM prototypes), PINNs (several groups at SNS and ESS), and RL (Kain+2020, Hirlaender+2020) are all active research directions with published results. The key message: the gap between today's lecture and the frontier is smaller than students often assume. Bubble position is schematic — readiness is illustrative, not a formal TRL score.
:::

## Summary

| | Tool | Key result |
|---|---|---|
| **RF fault detection** | Autoencoder (unsupervised) | ROC-AUC = 1.000, no fault labels |
| **Beam tuning** | Bayesian opt. + Cheetah | 13.2→2.2 mm, ~60 noisy evals, scales to high-D |
| **Surrogate model** | MLP, Tanh, normalised I/O | R²=1.00, **~600× speedup** |
